title: Los Usos de Haber — Practice
description: Authored B1 practice set for haber: hay vs está/están for existence vs location, hay always singular, hay que for impersonal obligation, había vs hubo, and haber as the auxiliary of the perfect tenses.

lessons.summary: Haber wears three hats. EXISTENCE: hay = there is / there are — and it stays singular whatever follows: 'Hay un parque', 'Hay muchos niños' (never «hayn»). The split with estar: hay introduces something NEW and indefinite ('Hay una farmacia cerca'), está/están locates something already known and definite ('La farmacia está en la esquina') — so hay never takes el/la or a name. In the past, había describes the scene ('Había mucha gente'), hubo reports an occurrence ('Hubo un apagón'). OBLIGATION: hay que + infinitive = one must, impersonally — 'Hay que cambiar el pañal' says the nappy needs changing without pointing at anyone (compare tener que, which names the person: 'Tengo que cambiarlo'). AUXILIARY: haber builds the perfect tenses with a participle — he comido, has estado, hemos dormido, había salido — and nothing can slip between them ('He comido ya', never «he ya comido»).

examples.spanish: Hay una plaza con juegos cerca de casa.
examples.english: There's a playground near our place.

examples.spanish: La plaza está al lado del mercado.
examples.english: The playground is next to the market.
There are lots of kids today.

examples.spanish: Todavía no ha dicho su primera palabra.
examples.english: He hasn't said his first word yet.

items.promptEnglish: Is there a pharmacy around here?
items.explanation: Asking whether something exists (indefinite: una farmacia) takes hay.

items.prompt: La farmacia ___ en la esquina, al lado del café.
items.promptEnglish: The pharmacy is on the corner, next to the café.
items.explanation: A known, definite thing (LA farmacia) is located with estar — hay can't take el/la.

items.prompt: Hoy ___ muchos niños en la plaza.
items.promptEnglish: There are lots of kids at the playground today.
items.explanation: Hay is invariable — singular or plural, it's always hay. «Hayn» doesn't exist.

items.prompt: ___ que cambiar el pañal antes de salir. (haber, presente)
items.promptEnglish: The nappy needs changing before we go out.
items.explanation: Hay que + infinitive: impersonal obligation, nobody named.

items.prompt: ¿Cuál dice que TE toca a ti hacerlo?
items.promptEnglish: Which one says it's YOUR job to do it?
items.explanation: Tener que names the person (tengo = I); hay que leaves it impersonal.

items.prompt: ___ mucha gente en el mercado esta mañana. (haber, descripción en pasado)
items.promptEnglish: There were a lot of people at the market this morning.
items.explanation: Scene description in the past → había (imperfect). And still singular: había mucha gente.

items.promptEnglish: Last night there was a huge storm.
items.explanation: A completed occurrence — something that happened — takes hubo (preterite).
The perfect builds on haber: ha + dicho. (Dicho is the irregular participle of decir.)
Nosotros auxiliary is hemos: hemos dormido. «Habemos» isn't standard.
Nothing squeezes between haber and the participle: ya goes outside — ya he comido.

items.prompt: Cuando llegamos, el médico ya ___ salido. (haber, pluscuamperfecto)
items.promptEnglish: When we arrived, the doctor had already left.
items.explanation: Past-before-past: había + participle (the pluperfect rides on haber too).

items.prompt: En la heladera no ___ nada para la cena.
items.promptEnglish: There's nothing in the fridge for dinner.
items.explanation: Existence (or here, absence) of something indefinite → hay. «La heladera no tiene nada» works too, but with no subject stated it's hay.
